restatements.text: Names the measure the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Provides the short title for the Act.
Lists findings regarding federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal, public schools, and CalFresh, and notes the concentration of wealth among California billionaires.
Declares the intent to fund health care, education, and food assistance through a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.

Amends the California Constitution to authorize a one-time tax on personal property and wealth of billionaires. Creates the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, allocating 90% to a Health Account and 10% to an Education and Food Assistance Account. Exempts these revenues from existing constitutional spending limits and formulas.

Adds to the Government Code the procedures for the Reserve Fund. Specifies the types of health, education, and food programs that can be funded. Sets annual appropriation limits. Requires a $50 million initial loan to the Franchise Tax Board for administration. Mandates annual reporting from the Department of Finance.
Names Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation Code.

Imposes a 5% excise tax for tax year 2026 on the net worth of individuals and applicable trusts with a net worth of $1 billion or more, phasing in the rate starting at $1 billion. Allows payment in five annual installments with a 7.5% deferral charge.
Specifies which debts and liabilities may reduce net worth, explicitly excluding debts to related persons, contingent debts, and charitable pledges made after October 15, 2025.

Establishes valuation methods for assets. Excludes real property, specific pensions, and up to $5 million in art or collectibles. Sets a formula for valuing private business interests using book value and profits unless a certified appraisal is provided.
Creates an Optional Deferral Account (ODA) allowing taxpayers whose tax liability exceeds their publicly traded assets to defer the tax, paying a 5% tax on later withdrawals or distributions.
Allows the Franchise Tax Board to penalize appraisers for substantial or gross overstatements or understatements of valuation in a certified appraisal.
Apportions 100% of the tax to California for residents, while allowing alternative apportionment if a taxpayer proves the wealth was not accumulated or sustained in the state.
Allows a pro rata credit for net wealth taxes paid to other jurisdictions.
Defines key terms, establishing the tax obligation date as January 1, 2026, and the valuation date as December 31, 2026.
Grants the Franchise Tax Board authority to adopt regulations and explicitly exempts the Board from the Administrative Procedure Act until January 1, 2028.
Permits the Legislature to amend the Act by a two-thirds vote, provided the amendment is consistent with and furthers the Act's purposes.
Includes a severability clause and instructs courts to reform dates or periods to preserve the tax if specific dates are found unconstitutional.
Imposes penalties of 20% for substantial tax understatements and 40% for gross understatements. Codifies economic substance and step transaction doctrines to prevent tax avoidance.
Requires the provisions to be liberally construed.
Authorizes an expedited judicial review process through a validation action filed solely in Sacramento County Superior Court, with direct appeal to the California Supreme Court.
Prohibits the state net worth tax from being deducted against state income taxes.
Declares that this measure prevails over any conflicting billionaire wealth tax measure on the same ballot.
Grants standing to the proponent and citizens to defend the Act in court if the Attorney General does not.

evidence.quote: the fair market value of those interests at the end of any tax year shall be presumed to be the sum of the book value of the business entity... plus a present-value multiplier of 7.5 times the annual book profits of the business entity
evidence.why: It introduces a complex valuation formula relying on specific accounting multiples for certain private business interests.

evidence.quote: The Board shall develop an optional deferral account contract and related forms for an optional deferral account, also referred to herein as an “ODA,”
evidence.why: It creates a complex, alternative mechanism for deferring and tracking tax obligations over time for specific illiquid assets.

evidence.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026 on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth by applicable individuals with net worth of $1 billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) or more
evidence.why: It specifically targets the wealthiest individuals by applying a 5% net worth tax exclusively to those with a net worth over $1 billion.

evidence.quote: a taxpayer must report the fair market value of those assets, and for each asset or group of substantially interchangeable assets (such as derivative contracts relating to the same underlying security) worth in excess of $1 million ($1,000,000), the taxpayer shall submit a certified appraisal.
evidence.why: It mandates the disclosure of highly detailed personal financial holdings and appraised values to the state.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to any regulation, standard, criterion, procedure, determination, rule, notice, guideline, or any other guidance established or issued by the Board pursuant to this Part.
evidence.why: It vastly expands the regulatory reach of the Franchise Tax Board by allowing it to issue binding rules without the standard public constraints of the Administrative Procedure Act.

evidence.quote: Ninety percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Health Account for health care funding, which may include expenditures to restore or address any reductions in federal funding or state appropriations; investments to protect or enhance Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs
evidence.why: It dedicates massive new funding specifically to maintain and expand Medi-Cal and health safety-net programs.

evidence.quote: For all sole proprietorships, all assets owned by or held through a sole proprietorship shall be reported and valued as though they were directly owned and held by the taxpayer... a taxpayer must report the fair market value of those assets, and for each asset or group of substantially interchangeable assets (such as derivative contracts relating to the same underlying security) worth in excess of $1 million ($1,000,000), the taxpayer shall submit a certified appraisal.
evidence.why: It requires business owners to comply with extensive new reporting and certified appraisal mandates for their private entities and sole proprietorships.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to any regulation, standard, criterion, procedure, determination, rule, notice, guideline, or any other guidance established or issued by the Board pursuant to this Part.
evidence.why: It removes standard legislative and public checks on regulatory rulemaking, shifting unconstrained immediate authority to an appointed tax board.

evidence.quote: the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth, whether tangible or intangible, and allows for the classification of personal property and wealth for differential taxation or for exemption, for the purpose of imposing the one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
evidence.why: It subjects the ownership of private property and accumulated assets directly to taxation.

evidence.quote: Food assistance expenditures to restore or address any reductions in federal funding or state appropriations, or further investments in programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood or California’s Universal Meals Program for school meals.
evidence.why: It directly allocates new state funding to critical food assistance programs for families, including Universal School Meals and CalFresh.

evidence.quote: the Department of Finance, in consultation with relevant state agencies, shall provide to the Legislature all the following information: (1) The current balance in the Reserve Fund... (7) Acertification that moneys from the Reserve Fund are not being used to supplant or replace state funding
evidence.why: It mandates annual, itemized public reporting on the new tax fund balances, spending, and requires a certification that funds are not replacing existing spending.

evidence.quote: The appropriation of funds from this measure shall not be used to supplant existing state funds for health care, education, or food assistance programs.
evidence.why: It guarantees that the new tax revenues will add to, rather than replace, existing state investments in these set program areas.

evidence.quote: the Reserve Fund is a special fund, permanently separate and apart from the General Fund or any other state fund or account. The taxes and the moneys resulting from the Act shall not be considered to be part of the General Fund
evidence.why: It locks the generated revenue into dedicated special funds that lawmakers cannot repurpose for other general needs.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to any regulation, standard, criterion, procedure, determination, rule, notice, guideline, or any other guidance established or issued by the Board pursuant to this Part.
evidence.why: It grants the appointed Franchise Tax Board the power to establish sweeping new rules uninhibited by legislative procedure or typical voter oversight.

evidence.quote: Ten percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account for education-related and food assistance expenditures, which may include: (A) Education-related expenditures... to make investments to protect or enhance the kindergarten through grade fourteen public education system.
evidence.why: It dedicates a permanent funding stream specifically for public school systems.

evidence.quote: The penalty for a substantial understatement under this Section shall be an amount equal to 20 percent of any understatement of tax.
evidence.why: It establishes severe new financial penalties against taxpayers for underreporting their net worth.

evidence.quote: the Board may at its discretion impose a penalty on the appraiser... no such penalty shall exceed 2 percent of the understatement of tax
evidence.why: It subjects professional appraisers to civil penalties and exposure for the valuations they issue.

evidence.quote: The penalty for a substantial understatement under this Section shall be an amount equal to 20 percent of any understatement of tax.
evidence.why: It expands the state's power to penalize taxpayers up to 20% to 40% for understating their wealth tax liability.

evidence.quote: the Board may at its discretion impose a penalty on the appraiser... no such penalty shall exceed 2 percent of the understatement of tax
evidence.why: It grants state agencies the authority to directly penalize private appraisers whose assessments are deemed substantial understatements.

evidence.quote: All revenues from the Act—including taxes, interest, and penalties, and less refunds—shall be deposited in the State Treasury... the Controller shall allocate and transfer the remaining moneys in the Reserve Fund to the following sub-accounts... 90% to the Billionaire Tax Health Account and 10% to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account.
evidence.why: It secures extensive new funding for state-level health care, education, and food programs.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to any regulation, standard, criterion, procedure, determination, rule, notice, guideline, or any other guidance established or issued by the Board pursuant to this Part.
evidence.why: It expands the regulatory and rulemaking power of the state Franchise Tax Board by exempting it from normal statutory checks for two years.

evidence.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026 on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth by applicable individuals with net worth of $1 billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) or more
evidence.why: It imposes a substantial new tax obligation directly on households who meet the wealth threshold.

evidence.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026 on the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth by applicable individuals with net worth of $1 billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) or more
evidence.why: It applies a unique tax bracket exclusively to those with net worth exceeding $1 billion, rather than applying an equal rate to everyone.

evidence.quote: Until January 1, 2028, the rulemaking provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 11340) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply
evidence.why: It removes legislative checks on executive rulemaking by suspending the Administrative Procedure Act for the Franchise Tax Board.

evidence.quote: Any appeal from an adverse determination in the Sacramento County Superior Court shall be directly to the California Supreme Court, without intermediate appellate review
evidence.why: It alters standard judicial checks by completely bypassing the appellate court system for validation actions.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. This measure establishes a first-of-its-kind state wealth tax by imposing a one-time 5% excise tax on the net worth of applicable individuals exceeding $1 billion.

Direct costs include $50 million loaned to the Franchise Tax Board to implement the tax. Indirect costs include massive compliance burdens for billionaires who must hire specialized accountants and appraisers to value closely held businesses and private equity assets.

Approximately 200 billionaires residing in California pay the tax. The beneficiaries are low- and moderate-income Californians who use Medi-Cal and CalFresh, health safety-net providers, and public school students.

Targeted individuals will likely engage in intensive estate planning, asset restructuring, or attempt to change their state residency prior to the tax obligation date to minimize liability. Taxpayers with illiquid private assets will extensively utilize the Optional Deferral Account.

Addresses the severe budget pressures on the health and education safety nets caused by federal funding cuts, and simultaneously targets the perceived unequal taxation of massive wealth accumulations. The mechanism directly levies a tax on those wealth pools. However, the measure may create problems involving capital flight, severe valuation disputes, and massive litigation.

The Franchise Tax Board gains extraordinary, unchecked regulatory discretion to define and enforce valuation methodologies outside the usual Administrative Procedure Act limits. Health care providers, school districts, and safety-net advocacy organizations gain access to a massive dedicated funding stream.

The economic impact and administrative feasibility of wealth taxes are highly disputed. Some economists argue wealth taxes successfully extract substantial revenue with minimal economic distortion and address systemic inequality. Conversely, other economists argue they are administratively unworkable, generate far less revenue than projected, and cause severe capital flight that shrinks the broader tax base.

Substantial resources will be consumed in administration. The measure immediately directs $50 million to the Franchise Tax Board, but extensive ongoing state resources, outside counsel fees, and judicial time will be necessary to adjudicate the complex valuation disputes and inevitable constitutional challenges.

The measure adds sections to both the State Constitution and statutory codes. The Legislature can only amend it with a two-thirds vote, and any amendment must be "consistent with and furthers the purposes" of the Act.

flags.quote: If the Board determines that a transaction or series of transactions lack economic substance
flags.note: The determination of 'economic substance' grants significant discretion to the tax board.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution
flags.note: Broadly overrides existing state constitutional constraints on property taxation and revenue limits.

flags.quote: The Board shall have the authority to adopt regulations to implement, interpret, make specific, or otherwise carry out any provision of this Part.
flags.note: The actual functioning and detailed valuation rules for the wealth tax rely entirely on future Board regulations.

flags.quote: The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as “the Act,” are severable.
flags.note: Contains standard severability and also explicitly directs courts to reform specified dates if found unconstitutional.

flags.quote: An excise tax is imposed for tax year 2026
flags.note: The tax is a one-time levy on the single designated tax year, though payment can be installed over five years.

flags.quote: The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Imposes both a supermajority requirement and a stringent 'furthers the purposes' restriction on future legislative amendments.

flags.quote: (1) Ninety percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Health Account... (2) Ten percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account
flags.note: Bundles a new tax on billionaires with allocations for health care, public schools, and food assistance programs.
